lesson.9_1.title: Portfolio check-up and final quiz
lesson.9_1.gut.prompt: You have a portfolio and many months of choices behind you. Before the final quiz: which one habit would you keep?
lesson.9_1.gut.c1.label: Spend first, save what is left
lesson.9_1.gut.c1.result: That is how most months end with nothing saved. The game paid you to try the other way round.
lesson.9_1.gut.c2.label: Save first, then spend the rest
lesson.9_1.gut.c2.result: That one habit sits under everything else you built here.
lesson.9_1.gut.bridge: A quick look back, then ten questions from across the levels.
lesson.9_1.c1.text: You started with wants and goals, and learned to set savings aside first.
lesson.9_1.c2.text: You built a safety net: an emergency fund, and the choice of health cover.
lesson.9_1.c3.text: You saw what borrowing really costs, and how a credit score is earned.
lesson.9_1.c4.text: You tried deposits, gold, a mutual fund and shares, and watched them behave differently in good and bad years.
lesson.9_1.c5.text: And you practised spotting scams before they cost you. Everything here used practice money and pretend markets: assumptions, not promises.
lesson.9_1.portfolio: Open your portfolio for the last check-up: net worth, Money Health Score, emergency months, what you owe and your scam-safety record.
lesson.9_1.q1.prompt: Your emergency fund covers less than one month. Which move comes first?
lesson.9_1.q1.o1: Put more practice money into shares
lesson.9_1.q1.right: Yes. A safety net comes before growth, so a surprise does not force you to borrow or sell at a loss.
lesson.9_1.q1.wrong: Not quite. Shares can fall right when you need the money. Build the safety net first, then grow.
lesson.9_1.q2.prompt: After this game, you know exactly how your real money will grow.
lesson.9_1.q2.right: Right, that is false. The game used pretend rates and markets. Real returns change and can be negative.
lesson.9_1.q2.wrong: Not quite. Everything here used assumptions, not promises. Real returns change and can be negative.
lesson.9_1.q3.prompt: Which habit is worth keeping from this journey?
lesson.9_1.q3.o1: Save a fixed amount first, then spend the rest
lesson.9_1.q3.o2: Spend first and save whatever is left
lesson.9_1.q3.right: Yes. Paying yourself first is the habit that makes the rest possible.
lesson.9_1.q3.wrong: Not quite. If you spend first, there is usually nothing left. Save first, then spend.
lesson.9_1.fq1.prompt: Your practice money arrives. What does "pay yourself first" mean?
lesson.9_1.fq1.o1: Buy what you want first, save what is left
lesson.9_1.fq1.o2: Set aside your savings first, then spend the rest
lesson.9_1.fq1.o3: Lend it to a friend first
lesson.9_1.fq1.right: Yes. Saving first is what makes sure saving happens at all.
lesson.9_1.fq1.wrong: It means setting savings aside before spending. "Whatever is left" is usually nothing.
lesson.9_1.fq2.prompt: You must enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
lesson.9_1.fq2.right: Correct, it's false. A PIN only ever sends money out.
lesson.9_1.fq2.wrong: It's false. Receiving needs nothing from you. If a screen asks for your PIN, money is about to leave.
lesson.9_1.fq3.prompt: Where does an emergency fund belong?
lesson.9_1.fq3.o1: In a savings account you can reach today
lesson.9_1.fq3.o2: In a deposit locked for five years
lesson.9_1.fq3.right: Yes. Emergency money must be easy to reach and must not swing in value.
lesson.9_1.fq3.wrong: An emergency cannot wait for a lock to open or a market to recover. Keep this money easy to reach.
lesson.9_1.fq4.prompt: You borrow ₹6,000 for 6 months at 18% a year. The EMI is about ₹1,053 and you repay about ₹6,319 in all. What did the loan cost you?
lesson.9_1.fq4.right: Yes. Total repaid minus the amount borrowed: about ₹319.
lesson.9_1.fq4.wrong: The cost of a loan is everything you repay minus what you borrowed: ₹6,319 − ₹6,000 = about ₹319.
lesson.9_1.fq5.prompt: Paying only the minimum due clears a credit card bill.
lesson.9_1.fq5.right: Correct, it's false. The minimum only avoids the late fee. Interest is charged on the rest.
lesson.9_1.fq5.wrong: It's false. The minimum due keeps the late fee away, but the unpaid part keeps growing with interest.
lesson.9_1.fq6.prompt: Your savings earn 3% a year. Prices rise 6% a year. What happens to what your money can buy?
lesson.9_1.fq6.right: Yes. The real return is 3% − 6% = −3%, so the money buys a little less each year.
lesson.9_1.fq6.wrong: Real return = return − inflation. Here that is −3%, so buying power shrinks.
lesson.9_1.fq7.prompt: Income tax is charged at one rate on every rupee a person earns.
lesson.9_1.fq7.right: Correct, it's false. Income is taxed in slabs, and each slab has its own rate.
lesson.9_1.fq7.wrong: It's false. Income is split into slabs, and each slab has its own rate. Only the income inside a slab is taxed at that slab's rate.
lesson.9_1.fq8.prompt: A mutual fund guarantees the return it earned last year.
lesson.9_1.fq8.right: Correct, it's false. A fund's value moves with the market. No return is promised.
lesson.9_1.fq8.wrong: It's false. Past returns are not a promise. A fund can earn less, or lose value.
lesson.9_1.fq9.o1: Putting everything into whatever rose most last year
lesson.9_1.fq9.o2: Spreading money across different kinds of asset
lesson.9_1.fq9.right: Yes. Spreading money means one fall cannot sink everything.
lesson.9_1.fq9.wrong: Diversification is spreading money across different kinds of asset, so one bad year does not hit all of it.
lesson.9_1.fq10.prompt: A message says: "Double your money in 25 days, guaranteed. Pay ₹2,000 to join." What is the safe reading?
lesson.9_1.fq10.o2: A scam: nobody can guarantee that
lesson.9_1.fq10.o3: Fine, if a friend forwarded it
lesson.9_1.fq10.right: Yes. A guaranteed, very high return plus a payment to join are both warning signs.
lesson.9_1.fq10.wrong: "Guaranteed" and "double" together are the warning. Do not pay; check who is registered, and report it.
